newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN urges Rwanda to ensure genocide trials are fair.
newsitem.headline: UN urges Rwanda to ensure genocide trials are fair.

text.p: The U.N. human rights office voiced concern on Thursday at lack of defence lawyers and delays in Rwanda's trials for more than 100,000 jailed Hutus accused of taking part in the 1994 genocide.

Out of 52 defendants tried since late 1996, 32 have been sentenced to death for involvement in the genocide of more than half a million minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs, it said in a statement.
But it said defence witnesses rarely appeared in court and lawyers did not represent civil claimants in most proceedings, likened by some Western legal experts to kangaroo trials.

The U.N. human rights office said it was worried about the security of lawyers, prosecutors, judges and witnesses. It said more than half of 250 newly-trained police investigators had quit because of fears over security or because of low pay.
It urged the government to release detainees who appeared to be facing charges of crimes against property.
Rwanda lost three quarters of all its judges in the genocide and has been trying to build its paralysed justice system from scratch.

The delay in trials is part of a larger and very emotional debate on justice in Rwanda. How much the government is prepared to forgive is a sensitive issue for survivors of the massacres, many of whom want an eye for an eye.
Many ordinary people were involved in the genocide and defendants are often presumed guilty unless proved innocent.
Few Hutus in jail have documents to indicate when they were arrested and by whom. Legal experts say it will not be possible to reconstruct their files, given the huge number of detainees.
